study.title: Heavy 45-s calf isometrics gave no immediate pain relief in mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy

full_text.why: Read in full from the free full text (PMC6706360, CC BY 4.0), extracted section by section.

key_findings: Rio's patellar dose (5 × 45 s at 70% MVC, 2 min rest) applied to the Achilles
Hop/heel-raise pain didn't drop: 4.2 to 4.9/10 in those with pain
95% CI rules out a 2-point mean drop straight after the holds
Pressure pain threshold and eccentric or fast concentric torque unchanged
Slow concentric torque up 5.9 Nm, below the 12.7 Nm MDC
summary: Single-session pre–post study, 16 adults (mean 48.6 y) with chronic unilateral mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy
No control group, no blinding, registration not reported; only 9 were painful on functional testing
Directly tests the immediate-analgesia claim for isometrics in the Achilles, and doesn't support it
Authors don't recommend heavy 45-s holds for immediate relief as first-stage rehab
Says nothing about isometrics as a loading programme over weeks
study.bottom_line: Don't sell calf isometrics as instant pain relief for mid-portion Achilles pain. If you use them, use them as tolerable early loading, judged on 24-hour response, not on what the hop feels like immediately after.

key_numbers.label: Functional pain NRS before vs after holds
Mean age, vs 22.5 and 26.9 y in Rio

setting: University lab; site and country not stated
participants: Unilateral mid-portion tendinopathy over 3 months, ultrasound-confirmed
VISA-A 61.3; no current or prior treatment
intervention: 5 × 45 s isometric plantar flexion at 70% MVC
Seated, hip and knee 90°, ankle 10° plantar flexed
Real-time force feedback on a Wii-board dynamometer
methods.follow_up: Retested immediately after the fifth hold; no later follow-up
primary_outcome: Pain NRS 0–10 on first painful task
Tasks: bilateral heel raises, then single-leg raises, then single-leg hops
Also pressure pain threshold and isokinetic torque

results.detail: Pain analysis appears to use the 9 symptomatic participants (n not labelled in Table 3). Narrative: those under 4/10 fell about 1 point, higher scorers seemed worse. MCID borrowed from chronic pain research (Farrar 2001), cited by the authors.

results.meaning: No local hypoalgesia; no MCID available
results.detail: Results text gives a different figure, −32.4 (−46.3 to 111.0), conflicting with the table. Measured with an electronic von Frey device at the most tender point, mean of 3 readings.

results.effect: Pre minus post −5.9 Nm (95% CI −11.4 to 0.33)
results.meaning: CI excludes the 12.7 Nm MDC; within measurement error
results.detail: The printed CI crosses zero yet p = 0.039, an internal inconsistency. 2 of 16 exceeded the MDC on visual inspection. MDC from Al-Uzri, cited by the authors.
Eccentric 98.5 to 106.0 Nm; concentric 225°/s 33.6 to 33.4 Nm. Effect sizes not reported for any outcome.

pico.p: 16 adults (mean 48.6 y) with chronic unilateral mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy, recruited from running clubs
pico.i: One session of 5 × 45 s isometric plantar flexion at 70% MVC, 2 min rest
pico.o: Immediate pain on heel raise/hop, pressure pain threshold, isokinetic plantar flexor torque

limits: No control group: can't separate effect from retesting or expectation
Only 9 of 16 had pain on testing
Immediate retest only; no 24-hour or multi-week data
Pressure pain figures conflict between table and text
One dose and position tested; others might differ
how_to_apply: Don't promise immediate pain relief from calf isometrics.
Don't use an immediate hop or heel-raise retest to judge isometrics.
If isometrics suit an irritable early patient, frame them as tolerable loading.
Judge loading by next-morning pain and stiffness, not in-session change.
Keep progressing towards isotonic calf loading as tolerated.
applies_to: Chronic mid-portion Achilles tendinopathy in recreational runners
Middle-aged adults with moderate VISA-A deficit
Choosing what to tell patients about isometrics
not_for: Patellar tendinopathy or young jumping athletes
Other isometric doses, angles or loads

grade.reason: Uncontrolled pre–post, unblinded, positive expectation script.
Same condition, dose and acute question; older runners than many sports caseloads.
Pain data from about 9 people; CI excludes a 2-point drop but far below optimal information size.
Null result published; not formally assessable for one study.

clinical_significance: Pain: CI upper limit of improvement 0.49 points, under the 2-point MCID (Farrar 2001, chronic pain)
So a meaningful average immediate drop is unlikely in this sample
Individual responders can't be ruled out with about 9 painful participants
Torque gain 5.9 Nm sits inside the 12.7 Nm MDC; no NNT derivable
comparator_fairness: Expectation was primed in favour of isometrics, which should have helped them
alternative_explanations: Null pain result despite positive priming argues against a hidden placebo boost
Torque rise may be learning or warm-up from repeated testing
Testing stopped at first painful task, so floor and ceiling effects possible
Age and chronicity (mean ~4 y) may blunt any acute response
spin: Little: conclusions match the null primary outcome
'Cannot be recommended' is strong for about 9 with no control
Significant torque result correctly flagged as below MDC
fit_with_evidence: Fits Clifford 2020 BMJ Open SEM review: isometrics not superior to isotonic, even immediately
Supports the Atlas line: load for adaptation, not for instant relief
external_validity: ✓ Recreational runners with chronic mid-portion pain
✓ Same dose clinicians copied from Rio
✗ Older (48.6 y) than young jumping athletes
✗ Chronic (mean ~4 y), not early-stage or irritable
would_change_my_mind: A controlled crossover in Achilles showing a 2-point drop vs isotonic
Data in acute, highly irritable or younger athletes showing relief
Multi-week trial showing isometrics beat isotonic for early pain
strengths: Directly tests the Rio dose in the Achilles
Uses MCID and MDC to interpret results
weaknesses: Table–text conflict for pressure pain threshold
appraisal.funding_conflicts: No funding. Authors declare no conflicts of interest.

Table 3 gives no n per row.
disagreements.resolved: Agreed: key number now '9 of 16 had pain'; n described as about 9.

disagreements.why: Printed CI includes zero and excludes the 12.7 Nm MDC.
disagreements.resolved: Agreed: no_difference; p/CI conflict kept in detail.

external.note: Single-group pre-post study; PEDro indexes trials and reviews only.
Review conclusion, isometrics not superior to isotonic even immediately, matches this card.

verification.external_searched: PEDro title search: not indexed. Web search for Cochrane or other reviews rating it: none. Clifford 2020 review read as abstract (PMC captcha).

study.patient_explanation: Holding a heavy calf contraction doesn't seem to switch Achilles pain off straight away. It can still be a gentle way to start loading the tendon. What matters is how the tendon feels the next morning and how it adapts over weeks.
open_questions: Do isometrics relieve pain in acute, highly irritable Achilles presentations?
Does a lower load or longer hold behave differently?
Is next-day tendon response better after isometric or isotonic early loading?
Do younger athletes respond like Rio's patellar group?
study.evidence_note: Small uncontrolled study; with Clifford 2020 it undercuts the immediate-analgesia rationale for isometrics.
study.confidence_note: Full text read via structured extraction, not verbatim; numbers cross-checked across 4 passes. Pain n inferred as 9.
study.impact_line: Stop promising instant relief from calf isometrics; use them as tolerable early loading, judged by next-day response.
